structure.title: Act I · Alexandria and Rome · An absence needs explaining
structure.text: Roman soldiers watch Antony in Egypt and decide what his love has done to their general. Cleopatra meanwhile wants him to measure how much he loves her. The same moment has different spectators and quite incompatible standards of measurement.

structure.title: Act II – Act III, scene 6 · Alliances · A marriage crosses the sea
structure.text: Antony must return to Roman business. A marriage promises to bind two rivals politically, and news of it travels to Alexandria. Diplomacy creates situations in which an absent person's height, expression or tone of voice can become a matter of state.

structure.title: Act III, scene 7 – Act V · War · Decisions under observation
structure.text: As rivalry becomes open conflict, the action cuts between ships, camps and palaces. Allies must decide whether yesterday's commander can still command tomorrow. The lovers contend over who will tell the story of their actions, even as the power to stage that story narrows.

people.name: Cleopatra
people.text: She can make a messenger's entrance into a theatrical event. The extravagance of her performances can obscure a precise political concern. She knows exactly what it would mean to become somebody else's spectacle in Rome.

people.name: Antony and Octavius Caesar
people.role: Partners in ruling the Roman world
people.text: Antony's standing draws upon victories and intense personal loyalties. Caesar has a particular gift for making a rival's pleasure look like neglect of duty. An apparent contrast between temperaments proves a powerful way of campaigning for power.

people.name: Enobarbus
people.text: He supplies the celebrated account of Cleopatra's arrival by barge. He also has to make practical decisions about a commander whose great moments he can describe more beautifully than anyone else.

context.title: Two places, many definitions
context.text: Rome and Egypt are places with interests, fleets and dependent populations. Characters also use their names as shorthand for discipline or pleasure. The people living in them are considerably less consistent than those convenient national descriptions.

notice.text: Watch a messenger trying to finish a sentence.
notice.why: Cleopatra may interrupt the news to question the physical details of the person delivering it. How much information survives the journey depends partly on what a frightened subordinate dares to repeat.

notice.text: Who describes the lovers while they are offstage?
notice.why: Memories and hostile reports can command the scene in their absence. A legend takes shape from accounts supplied by friends and enemies who need the lovers to mean different things.

opening: Antony has responsibilities across the Roman world and an excellent reason to neglect them in Egypt. Cleopatra makes being with her feel grander than the business calling him away, but neither lover can stop being a ruler long enough to become merely private. Shakespeare gives their attraction the extravagance of people accustomed to changing other lives with a decision. Pleasure, jealousy, strategy, and performance become difficult to separate when the relationship everyone is gossiping about can also alter who governs an empire.
